477.title: A field in wartime (Jeremiah 32:6–15)
477.hook: with the enemy at the gates, Jeremiah buys land: houses will be bought here again
477.howItsDone: Christians often turn to Jeremiah 32 in times of crisis as a picture of hope that acts, and preachers have used it in wartime, in economic downturns and when churches build or plant in struggling neighborhoods.

segments.voice: Yesterday, a new covenant, God's teaching written inside, and your line: on the heart.

A real estate agent calls during a war. The enemy army is camped around your city. Siege ramps are going up against the walls. Food is running out. And the agent says: there's a field for sale, just outside town. Actually, it's behind enemy lines right now. Interested? It sounds like a joke. Jeremiah said yes. He was under arrest at the time, held in the guard's courtyard of the king's palace, for saying out loud that Babylon would win. And his cousin came to see him with exactly that offer.
screen: `A CITY UNDER SIEGE.` → `JEREMIAH UNDER ARREST.` → `A FIELD FOR SALE.`

segments.voice: It's the tenth year of King Zedekiah. The Babylonian army surrounds Jerusalem. Jeremiah's cousin Hanameel comes and says: buy my field at Anathoth, our home village; the right to redeem it is yours. In Israel's law, when family land was about to be lost, a close relative had the right, and the duty, to buy it back so it stayed in the family. God had told Jeremiah this visit was coming. So Jeremiah does it, and does it properly. He weighs out seventeen shekels of silver. He signs the deed and calls witnesses. He makes two copies, one sealed and one open, and hands them to his scribe, Baruch, to put in a clay jar so they'll last a long time. Why the jar? Because he isn't buying for this year. He's buying for after. And he says why, in the King James Bible: "For thus saith the LORD of hosts, the God of Israel; Houses and fields and vineyards shall be possessed again in this land." This is the prophet who has warned for years that the city will fall. He hasn't changed his message. But he puts his money on the far side of the fall. Then he prays, and admits it seems absurd: the city is being handed to the Chaldeans, and you told me to buy a field. He begins: "Ah Lord GOD! behold, thou hast made the heaven and the earth by thy great power and stretched out arm, and there is nothing too hard for thee." Hope, here, isn't a feeling. It's a signed deed in a clay jar.
screen: `THE ARMY AT THE WALLS.` · `THE RIGHT TO REDEEM IS YOURS.` · `SEVENTEEN SHEKELS, A DEED, A JAR.` · `HOPE AS A SIGNED DEED.` · then, large: `FIELDS SHALL BE POSSESSED AGAIN.`

segments.voice: Think of something in your world that feels besieged, your health, your town, a relationship, the news, and don't pretend it's fine; Jeremiah didn't. Then ask what small thing you could put on the far side of it, a tree to plant, a garden bed for next spring, a letter to your future self, and picture yourself signing the deed. If you pray, you can offer that hope to God, the way Jeremiah did.
Anathoth. Jeremiah's home village, where his cousin's field became a sealed deed bought under siege, a bet on the far side of the fall.
Your line: houses will be bought again. Hope, signed and sealed. Day four hundred seventy-seven, done.

478.title: Dry bones (Ezekiel 37:1–14)
478.hook: a valley of bones rattles together, and breath comes into them
478.howItsDone: Ezekiel 37 is read at the Easter Vigil and at Pentecost in many churches, and has long been sung and preached in African American churches as a vision of hope; in Jewish practice it is the prophetic reading on the Sabbath during Passover.

segments.voice: Yesterday, a field at Anathoth bought in wartime, and your line: houses will be bought again.

Jeremiah stayed in Jerusalem. Another prophet, Ezekiel, a priest, was among the exiles already taken to Babylon, living by a river there. His visions are strange and vast: wheels full of eyes, a scroll he's told to eat, a Temple measured out cubit by cubit. Then news reaches the exiles: Jerusalem has fallen. The Temple is gone. And the people say: our bones are dried up. Our hope is lost. We're cut off. Into that, Ezekiel is carried by the spirit and set down in a valley.
screen: `EZEKIEL AMONG THE EXILES.` → `JERUSALEM HAS FALLEN.` → `OUR HOPE IS LOST.` → `SET DOWN IN A VALLEY.`

segments.voice: In the King James Bible: "The hand of the LORD was upon me, and carried me out in the spirit of the LORD, and set me down in the midst of the valley which was full of bones." He's led around them: very many, and very dry. Long dead. And God asks: "Son of man, can these bones live?" Ezekiel's answer is careful, almost wise: "O Lord GOD, thou knowest." Not yes. Not no. Then God tells him to prophesy to the bones: "O ye dry bones, hear the word of the LORD." He does, and there's a noise, a rattling, and the bones come together, bone to his bone. Sinews, then flesh, then skin. But no breath. Bodies, lying there. So God tells him to prophesy a second time, to the breath: come from the four winds, O breath, and breathe on these slain. Breath comes into them, and they live, and stand up on their feet, an exceeding great army. The word that holds it together is the Hebrew ruach, all through this passage, meaning breath, and wind, and spirit, all at once. The spirit carries Ezekiel. The breath enters the bodies. The four winds supply it. One word, and English needs three. Then God explains: these bones are the whole house of Israel. They say our hope is lost. I will open your graves and bring you home. Jewish communities read this vision on the Sabbath during Passover, the festival of freedom. Christians also hear in it the hope of resurrection, and of the Spirit who gives life.

segments.voice: Breathe in deeply and feel the air arrive; you didn't make it. Then bring to mind something that feels like dry bones, a project, a hope, a friendship, a faith gone quiet, and ask Ezekiel's question honestly, can this live, without forcing an answer. With each breath in, picture breath moving toward it, and with each breath out, release your need to control it; if you pray, you can say: thou knowest.
Dry bones. Ezekiel's valley of the long dead, joined bone to bone and filled with breath: a picture of a people's hope coming back to life.
Your line: can these bones live? One word, ruach, for breath, wind and spirit. That's day four hundred seventy-eight.

479.title: A heart of flesh (Ezekiel 36:26)
479.hook: I will take out the heart of stone
479.howItsDone: Christians often pray Ezekiel 36:26 when asking God to change them, and it is read at the Easter Vigil, at confirmations and at services of renewal; it appears in many hymns and worship songs about the Spirit.

segments.voice: Yesterday, a valley of dry bones and breath blowing through them. Your line: can these bones live?

Stone doesn't feel anything. That's what makes it good for walls. A sibling, an old friend, a parent, a coworker: someone hurts a person enough times, and something in that person goes hard. The name pops up on a phone, and there's nothing, or worse, a cold click. It works like protection, and sometimes it is. But walls spread: harder with one person, then a little harder with everyone. Ezekiel had watched a whole people grow hard: toward God, toward the poor, toward the truth. And he heard a promise about the heart.
screen: `A NAME POPS UP.` → `A COLD CLICK.` → `THE HARDNESS SPREADS.`

segments.voice: In the King James Bible, God says through Ezekiel: "A new heart also will I give you, and a new spirit will I put within you: and I will take away the stony heart out of your flesh, and I will give you an heart of flesh." In the Hebrew Bible, the heart, lev, isn't mainly where you feel. It's often where people think, decide and choose: the whole inner self. So a heart of stone isn't just sadness. It's a self that can't be moved, taught or reached. A heart of flesh is alive again, soft enough to feel, to change, to care. The trade isn't weak for strong. It's stone for flesh. Flesh can be hurt, and that's the point: only something that can be hurt can also love. Now look back to chapter eighteen. There Ezekiel tells the people: make you a new heart and a new spirit. Make it yourselves. Here, God says: I will give it. So which is it? The book holds both. Some readers put it this way: the new heart is something you're called to reach for, and something you can only receive. Christians often connect this verse to the work of the Holy Spirit; Jewish readers hear God's promise to renew Israel after exile. Both hear the same image: stone taken out, flesh given back.
screen: `A NEW HEART WILL I GIVE YOU.` · `LEV: WHERE YOU THINK AND CHOOSE.` · `ONLY FLESH CAN BE HURT, OR LOVE.` · `MAKE IT, OR RECEIVE IT? BOTH.` · then, large: `AN HEART OF FLESH.`

segments.voice: Bring to mind someone you've gone hard toward; not the one who hurt you most, someone smaller. Notice the stone, the tight chest, the ready list of what they did, and set the list down for a minute while you see one ordinary, human thing about them: they get tired, they were a child once, someone they love is sick. Let your chest loosen by one degree, and if you pray, ask for a heart of flesh.
Lev. The Hebrew word for heart, the whole inner self: where you think, decide and choose, not only where you feel.
Your line: loosen by one degree. Stone can't love; flesh can. Day four hundred seventy-nine, done.

480.title: The fiery furnace (Daniel 3)
480.hook: three young men won't bow, and a fourth walks in the fire with them
480.howItsDone: The story of the three young men is a favorite in Sunday schools, and in Catholic, Orthodox and Anglican worship their song from the furnace, the Benedicite, is sung or said as a canticle; Orthodox Christians sing it in the Christmas season and at the Easter Vigil.

segments.voice: Yesterday, lev: a heart of stone traded for one of flesh. Your line: loosen by one degree.

A golden statue stands on a plain outside Babylon, sixty cubits high, ninety feet or so. King Nebuchadnezzar has gathered every official in his empire: governors, judges, treasurers. A herald shouts the rule. When the music starts, horns, pipes, harps, every kind of instrument, everyone falls down and worships the statue. Anyone who doesn't goes into a burning furnace. The music starts. Thousands drop to the ground at once. And three young men, Jewish exiles who've risen to high posts in Babylon, stay standing. In Babylon they're called Shadrach, Meshach and Abednego.
screen: `A GOLDEN STATUE ON A PLAIN.` → `WHEN THE MUSIC STARTS, BOW.` → `THREE MEN STAY STANDING.`

segments.voice: The furious king gives them one more chance. Their answer, in the King James Bible: "our God whom we serve is able to deliver us from the burning fiery furnace, and he will deliver us out of thine hand, O king. But if not, be it known unto thee, O king, that we will not serve thy gods." Hear the hinge: but if not. They believe God can save them. They don't claim to know he will. Their choice doesn't hang on the outcome. Enraged, the king has the furnace heated seven times hotter, so hot the soldiers who throw them in die in the flames. Then Nebuchadnezzar leaps up: "Lo, I see four men loose, walking in the midst of the fire, and they have no hurt; and the form of the fourth is like the Son of God." Four. Loose. Walking. They come out with not a hair singed, their clothes untouched, and, the text says, the smell of fire had not passed on them. Who is the fourth? The king himself says God sent his angel. In the original Aramaic he says the fourth looks like a son of the gods, how a Babylonian king might describe a heavenly being. Many Christians, from early on, have seen Christ there, the Son of God present before his birth; others see an angel, as the king says. Either way, they weren't kept out of the fire. Someone walked in it with them. Catholic and Orthodox Bibles also include the long song the three men sing in the flames.
screen: `BUT IF NOT.` · `SEVEN TIMES HOTTER.` · `FOUR MEN, LOOSE, WALKING.` · `NOT KEPT OUT, BUT ACCOMPANIED.` · then, large: `THE FORM OF THE FOURTH.`

segments.voice: Think of one small pressure to go along, a joke at someone's expense or a shortcut that isn't honest, and picture yourself standing, quietly, without drama. Notice the fear that comes with it, then picture not being alone in it. If you pray, ask for courage, and for company in the fire.
Bar elahin. Aramaic for a son of the gods: how the king described the fourth figure walking in the flames.
Your line: a fourth in the fire. Being in the fire doesn't mean being alone in it. See you tomorrow.

481.title: The lions' den (Daniel 6)
481.hook: Daniel prays at his window three times a day, law or no law
481.howItsDone: Some Christians keep fixed times of daily prayer, morning, midday and evening, through the Liturgy of the Hours, the Angelus, the Book of Common Prayer offices or simple personal habit; Jewish tradition prays three daily services, facing Jerusalem.

segments.voice: Yesterday, bar elahin: a fourth figure walking in the furnace. Your line: a fourth in the fire.

The lions' den often gets told as a young hero's story. Follow the book's own timeline instead. Daniel was carried off to Babylon as a youth. Now Babylon itself has fallen, and a new ruler, Darius, sits on the throne. Daniel has outlasted the kings who took him. After a lifetime in government, he's so honest and capable that Darius plans to set him over the whole kingdom. The other officials can't stand it. They hunt for corruption and find none. Finally they say: we'll never catch him, unless it's about the law of his God.
screen: `NOT A YOUNG HERO.` → `AN OLD, HONEST OFFICIAL.` → `NO CORRUPTION TO FIND.` → `A TRAP ABOUT HIS GOD.`

segments.voice: So they flatter the king: make a decree that for thirty days, no one may pray to any god or person except you. Break it, and you go to the lions. Darius signs, and by the law of the Medes and Persians it can't be changed. Now watch Daniel. In the King James Bible: "Now when Daniel knew that the writing was signed, he went into his house; and his windows being open in his chamber toward Jerusalem, he kneeled upon his knees three times a day, and prayed, and gave thanks before his God, as he did aforetime." As he did aforetime. No protest. No closed shutters either. He just keeps doing what he's always done, at a window facing a city he hasn't seen since he was young. The habit was already there; the law simply found it. Three times a day echoes a psalm: "Evening, and morning, and at noon, will I pray." Jewish tradition keeps three daily times of prayer, and synagogues traditionally face toward Jerusalem. The officials catch him. The king, who has set his heart on saving Daniel, tries until sundown and can't. Daniel goes in, and a stone seals the den. The king spends the night fasting and sleepless. At dawn he calls into the den: is thy God able to deliver thee from the lions? And from inside: "My God hath sent his angel, and hath shut the lions' mouths, that they have not hurt me." Christian readers often hear this as a call to steady, daily faithfulness, ready before the test comes.

segments.voice: Choose three moments in your day to pause, even for thirty seconds, after breakfast, at lunch, before sleep: three windows to turn your face toward. Then take the first pause now: be still, breathe, and give thanks for one thing. If you pray, pray as Daniel did, with thanks; if not, simply stop and notice.
Darius. The king who signed the decree that trapped Daniel, then spent a sleepless night trying to save the man he'd set over his kingdom.
Your line: the window stays open. The habit was there before the test came. That's day four hundred eighty-one.

482.title: I taught Ephraim to walk (Hosea 11:1–4)
482.hook: God as a parent holding a toddler's hands, bending down to feed
482.howItsDone: Christians read Hosea 11 in sermons and Bible study as a picture of God's parental love, and Matthew 2:15 quotes its first verse in the story of Jesus' childhood.

segments.voice: Yesterday, Darius and the lions' den, and Daniel's open window. Your line: the window stays open.

Watch a parent teach a toddler to walk. They crouch behind the child, one finger in each tiny fist, bent nearly double, back aching. The child has no idea anyone is holding on, thinks they're walking all alone, and that's the point. Later, the same parent leans down with a spoon, patient, while half of it lands on the floor. Somebody probably held each of us like that once, and nobody remembers it. An old prophet named Hosea reached for exactly this picture of God. Not a king on a throne. A parent on their knees in the hallway.

Hosea preached in the northern kingdom of Israel, and his book often calls the north Ephraim, after one of its tribes. In the King James Bible: "When Israel was a child, then I loved him, and called my son out of Egypt." The Exodus, remembered not as a battle but as a parent calling a child home. Then the toddler scene: "I taught Ephraim also to go, taking them by their arms; but they knew not that I healed them." That's the ache: held, fed and healed, and never noticed. Verse four: "I drew them with cords of a man, with bands of love." Not chains for an animal. Human cords, the kind a person uses to guide someone they love. Then a farmer's picture: God easing the yoke off their jaws and bending down to lay food before them. The chapter isn't sweet all the way through. Hosea names the people's turning away, and hard years coming. But a few verses later God says, in effect, my heart is turned within me; I can't give you up. The love outlasts the anger. Matthew's Gospel later borrows the first line, out of Egypt have I called my son, and hears it in the child Jesus and his family in Egypt. Christians who follow Matthew hear Hosea on two levels: Israel's story, and a pattern Jesus walks again. Either way, God in this book is the one on their knees.
screen: `OUT OF EGYPT: A PARENT CALLING HOME.`
`CORDS OF A MAN, BANDS OF LOVE.`
then, large: `I TAUGHT EPHRAIM ALSO TO GO.`

segments.voice: Picture the hands of someone who held you up before you could stand, even if you don't remember it; Hosea's point is that you probably wouldn't. Then think of a small one in your life now, a child, a pet, a seedling, a younger colleague finding their feet, and one small act of care you could give them. If you pray, give thanks for the hands that held you; if not, simply let the gratitude sit.

483.title: Your old men shall dream (Joel 2:28–29)
483.hook: I will pour out my spirit on all flesh; Peter quoted it at Pentecost
483.howItsDone: Some churches read Joel 2:28–29 near Pentecost, alongside Acts 2, where Peter quotes it; churches that keep the Christian year celebrate Pentecost seven weeks after Easter as the coming of the Holy Spirit.

segments.voice: Yesterday, ahavah: Hosea's parent on their knees, teaching Ephraim to walk. Your line: cords of love.

Nine in the morning in Jerusalem, a festival crowd in the streets, and a commotion. A small group of Jesus's followers pour out of a house, talking in languages they never learned, and visitors from many nations hear their own home tongues. Some are amazed; others laugh: they're drunk. Then Peter, a fisherman who not long before had denied he even knew Jesus, stands up. It's too early in the day for that, he says. And instead of explaining, he quotes an old prophet, from a book so short it's easy to flip past: Joel.
screen: `NINE IN THE MORNING, A FESTIVAL CROWD.`

segments.voice: Joel is only three or four chapters long, and nobody is sure exactly when he lived. His book opens with a disaster: locusts strip the land bare. He calls the people to fast and turn back to God, and then the promises come, rain and harvest, then something bigger. In the King James Bible: "I will pour out my spirit upon all flesh; and your sons and your daughters shall prophesy, your old men shall dream dreams, your young men shall see visions." Look at the list. Sons and daughters, not just sons. Old and young. Then further: "And also upon the servants and upon the handmaids in those days will I pour out my spirit." Servants. In earlier stories of the Hebrew Bible, the spirit comes on particular people: a judge like Gideon, a king like Saul, a prophet. Joel pictures it soaked into everyone, like rain on a field after the locusts. And old people dreaming means nobody has aged out of hearing from God. Now Acts chapter two. Peter tells the crowd: "But this is that which was spoken by the prophet Joel." Christians remember that day as Pentecost, and some call it the birthday of the church. Jews read Joel too, and hear his promise their own way, as a hope for Israel's renewal. For Christians, Peter's sermon made Joel's list the guest list of the church. This week brought a field bought in wartime, dry bones, a heart of flesh, a furnace, a lions' den, a child learning to walk, and now the spirit on everyone. Over and over, the prophets refuse to give up on people.
screen: then, large: `YOUR OLD MEN SHALL DREAM DREAMS.`

segments.voice: Picture the oldest person you know and the youngest. Ask when you last listened to either without correcting, what the old one might still be dreaming, and what the young one might be seeing that you've stopped seeing. If you pray, pray Joel's promise over them in its own words; if not, just hold them both for a moment.
Pentecost. The day Peter quoted Joel's promise that God's spirit would pour out on everyone, now remembered as the church's birthday.
Your line: on all flesh. Nobody ages out of hearing from God. Day four hundred eighty-three, and another week walked.
